verses.text: “Yes, at this my heart trembles, and is moved out of its place.
Hear, oh, hear the noise of his voice, the sound that goes out of his mouth.
He sends it out under the whole sky, and his lightning to the ends of the earth.
After it a voice roars. He thunders with the voice of his majesty. He doesn’t hold back anything when his voice is heard.
God thunders marvelously with his voice. He does great things, which we can’t comprehend.
For he says to the snow, ‘Fall on the earth;’ likewise to the shower of rain, and to the showers of his mighty rain.
He seals up the hand of every man, that all men whom he has made may know it.
Then the animals take cover, and remain in their dens.
Out of its room comes the storm, and cold out of the north.
By the breath of God, ice is given, and the width of the waters is frozen.
Yes, he loads the thick cloud with moisture. He spreads abroad the cloud of his lightning.
It is turned around by his guidance, that they may do whatever he commands them on the surface of the habitable world,
Whether it is for correction, or for his land, or for loving kindness, that he causes it to come.
“Listen to this, Job. Stand still, and consider the wondrous works of God.
Do you know how God controls them, and causes the lightning of his cloud to shine?
Do you know the workings of the clouds, the wondrous works of him who is perfect in knowledge?
You whose clothing is warm, when the earth is still by reason of the south wind?
Can you, with him, spread out the sky, which is strong as a cast metal mirror?
Teach us what we shall tell him, for we can’t make our case by reason of darkness.
Will it be told him that I would speak? Or should a man wish that he were swallowed up?
Now men don’t see the light which is bright in the skies, but the wind passes, and clears them.
Out of the north comes golden splendor. With God is awesome majesty.
We can’t reach the Almighty. He is exalted in power. In justice and great righteousness, he will not oppress.
Therefore men revere him. He doesn’t regard any who are wise of heart.”

footnotes.content: When the truth about God strikes us, the body answers before the mind does. Elihu speaks truly here—awe is not meant to stay in our thoughts. It shakes us to the bone because we glimpse, however dimly, the reality of the One who holds all things.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Sound carries presence. When you hear thunder far off, you know something real approaches. Elihu calls us to listen as we would to a voice speaking directly to us—because God's voice in creation is exactly that. Not distant. Not indifferent.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Notice the scope: not just one place, but the whole sky, the ends of the earth. God's word and power are not local—they reach everywhere, held in one coherent order. When we know this, our troubles find their right size.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "He doesn't hold back anything when his voice is heard." No restraint, no half-measure—that is the nature of God's power. And yet, for all its force, it serves: thunder announces rain to the thirsty earth, lightning clears the air. His unleashed power is always also mercy.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "He does great things, which we can't comprehend." After a lifetime, I've learned that this is not meant to humble us into silence. It calls us to wonder, to pay attention, to say yes to what we see even when we don't understand how it works. Understanding comes later, if at all.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: God's word spoken to creation: "Fall on the earth." Snow and rain obey as simply as Adam named the animals. The order that Elihu describes isn't harsh command but intimate knowing—God speaks to the weather as a gardener speaks to the garden, tending what He has made.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: In storm, all work stops. The hand is sealed—whether beggar's or king's, laborer's or merchant's. In that enforced rest, Elihu says, people know. Know what? That they are not in charge. That something greater holds the world. This too is mercy, hard-won.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Even the animals know when to hide. They read the weather in their bones and turn inward without argument. Sometimes wisdom looks like that: knowing when to stop, when to shelter, when to wait. The beasts teach us if we pay attention.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Storm comes out of its room, cold from the north. The text personifies wind as emerging from hidden chambers, as though the world has places we don't see where God's power gathers itself. There is more going on than meets the eye—always has been.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "By the breath of God, ice is given." When you see a frozen lake or icicles hanging still in winter dawn, you are looking at the Word made visible. Not distant doctrine but His breath, His will, holding water in a shape it wouldn't hold by itself.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Clouds laden with moisture, lightning spreading through them—Elihu traces how power moves through creation with almost a musician's eye for pattern. He's painting a picture so clear, so beautiful, that Job will have to look at the sky differently forever after.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Turned around by his guidance"—clouds don't drift randomly but move under direction, carrying out commands on the inhabited world below. The image is of perfect coordination, as if all creation is a choreography and God the choreographer who knows every step.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Rain may come for correction—drought broken by a storm, or flood as judgment. Or it comes for the land itself, for blessing and fruitfulness. Or for loving-kindness, pure gift. The same weather serves all these ends because the hand guiding it sees what each hour needs.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Listen to this, Job. Stand still, and consider." The word is an invitation, almost gentle after all the thunder and grandeur. Elihu isn't scolding—he's saying, 'Stop what you're doing. Look. Let your mind rest on how wonderful this all is.' That is how the Lord draws us back to Himself.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Do you know how He controls them? The honest answer is: not fully. We see effects—we see light, we see lightning, we see clouds move. But the mechanism? The why of it all? Only God holds that completely. And in not knowing, we are freed to trust.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Perfect in knowledge"—not just knowing the facts of cloud-working, but knowing how every drop serves the good of creation. That perfection is what separates God's use of power from all human use. He needs never harm what He does not intend to heal.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Even warmth—the comfort of good clothing while the earth is still—is part of the account. Elihu is not only painting the terrible beauty of God's power but the everyday mercy in it. We are meant to notice both the storm and the quiet day that follows it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Can you spread out the sky like a mirror of cast metal? The image is of something impossibly strong, impossibly smooth, impossibly perfect. The answer is no—we cannot. And in that humbled no, we find our place: creatures beneath a craftsmanship we cannot equal.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Teach us what we shall tell him." Job doesn't know how to speak to God. We often don't either—the right words feel impossible. But notice: Elihu's answer is not to coach the words but to shift the gaze. Stop preparing your case. Look at who you are before. That changes everything.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Should a man wish that he were swallowed up?" Here is the edge of Elihu's speech: wanting the ground to open? That is not faith; that is despair masked as piety. Yet even in rebuking it, Elihu shows compassion—he knows Job wants the noise to stop, the questions to end.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Cloud cover hides the sun, but wind clears it away. Light returns. After darkness, clarity—and it comes, Elihu says, naturally, as part of the order. Even our times of not-seeing are temporary. This is how God works: He hides and reveals in rhythm, like breath itself.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Golden splendor from the north—arctic light, perhaps, or the gleam of cleared skies and ice. Paired with "awesome majesty," Elihu shows that beauty and power are not opposites: God is both the terrible and the gorgeous, and both come from the same source.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "In justice and great righteousness, he will not oppress." After all the storm and awe, Elihu anchors the truth: power this great, held this perfectly, cannot be bent to wrong. God's might is never arbitrary. He cannot oppress because He is just by nature, not by choice.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "He doesn't regard any who are wise of heart." The proud, the self-assured, the ones who rest in their own understanding—God does not defend their position. But those who fear Him? They He honors. After all these verses of thunder and majesty, the final word is: He values reverence over cleverness.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
